title: Greenville restaurant cited for improper thawing, labeling methods - NewsBreak
text:
By A.J. Jackson ,
16 hours ago
One restaurant in Greenville County fell below the "78" food grade score threshold in April, while more than 30 other local diners and food trucks had perfect inspections found by the South Carolina Department of Agriculture (SCDA).
The statewide inspection team reported that the lone restaurant, which scored under 78, had improper thawing and labeling methods during its April check-in, but by the next week, it had regained its "A" grade.
In our coverage of food inspections around Greenville County, we will categorize violations into two types: priority and foundational. Priority violations are those that pose the highest risk of causing foodborne illness and identify contributing factors that could lead to illness. A priority foundation violation is a contributing factor that can cause illness.
According to SCDA reports for April, no other Greenville County restaurant, institution, or grocery store received a "C" rating that fell below 78 during their month-long roundups.
Here is a snapshot of the April food inspections for commercial dining establishments in Greenville County:

Core 450 (Restaurant) Location: 450 Cherokee Valley Way (Travelers Rest)
During routine inspections on April 9, SCDA found 13 out-of-compliance violations, including five foundation and five priority occurrences. Some of the most notable violations were:
observed excessive organic matter in the kitchen deli slicer observed deli meats, cooked ribs, chicken, and sauces in the walk-in cooler without proper date marking observed pork ribs in standing water observed no date marking system in place Initial score: 75 out of 100.
An official follow-up visit by SCDA was administered on April 14, during which the restaurant reestablishe d its "A" letter grade and a score of 100.
Since 2022, Core 45 has earned 11 "A" and three "B" grades in its inspections prior to the April 5 and April 17 reports.

The Agriculture Department performs more than 2,500 routine and follow-up procedures each year across the county.
To keep our food and dining readers informed, the Greenville News covers sanitation and health grades issued by the South Carolina Department of Agriculture (SCDA) for the food and dining industry. Overall inspection scores and letter grades are updated on the storefront immediately after an inspection.
On a scale of 100, food grades below 78 indicate that the food establishment's practices require significant improvement. During routine inspections, a "C" grade restaurant is classified as such, and 10 days later, it is followed up on to ensure changes are made.
